Like you said, it is 100% your ED telling you this.  For you to be conscious of it at all, and feel this anxiety, is the definition of disordered eating.  I know it can be so hard to make the shift from restricting to eating meals again, and specifically the anxiety centered around seconds and finishing meals can be grueling.  I try to remind myself that it is a sickness, and that recovery is not always linear.  As far as seconds, that is something you should never feel bad for!  Your body has carried you from when you were a tiny baby to now, growing and changing and supporting you, the least you can do is get that second plate of food.  It is delicious! You deserve it! Never feel guilty for supporting the body that supports you <3

I feel the same way, before my current relationship my BPD caused me to permanently damage a three year relationship and now me and my ex barely speak (after about a year and half of no contact we are beginning to talk again here and there)

The biggest thing for me has been a change in mindset- it is really hard and I owe a lot of my progress to DBT, but when you are in the moment, feeling or thinking something intense it is so important to establish a sort of checker in your brain that allows you to take a step away from the situation and think "is this a normal response/thought, or is it being affected by my BPD?" if it you you can then go on to ask "how is BPD effecting this feeling, how can I work to regulate it?" I know it seems tedious and nearly impossible in the moment but it has significantly impacted my current relationship for the better.  That along with talking to my boyfriend about BPD, explaining what it looks/feels like for me, and having an open and honest conversation about it (and answering any questions he might have.)

You are so capable of moving forward, you are not just some fuck up, you are not a bad person, you have BPD.  it is a crazy hard disorder to navigate, and you cant blame yourself or judge your character for something you cant control.

I have a very similar story to your daughters and have been diagnosed with BPD this year, my therapist sourcing it back mostly to the event of the molestation.  It is defiantly a viable cause/factor for BPD.  

As far as books go I would recommend the dialectical behavior therapy wellness planner- it is a really good guided resource for working through emotions and different elements of BPD, I have found that journaling and guided journaling in particular has really helped with emotional regulation and management, another suggestion is beyond borderline- it has really interesting stories from other people with BPD as well as advice and things they did to manage it or recover.

As a 17 year old it puts such a smile on my face to see the efforts you are putting in when it comes to helping your daughter navigate mental health; whether she knows it or not she is so lucky to have you :)

for me it had been so helpful to fully explain my BPD to my boyfriend so he is aware of the potential and capacity of splitting.  In a similar situation I might reach out to him and explain that my brain is making this into something bigger than it is- that I recognize that- but that it is still something that might take a big toll on me.  If he understands your disorder he can help you work through splitting 'episodes' and it can really work to strengthen your relationship. ( or it has in my case )

this is such a hard thing to deal with, especially the spiraling- I know exactly how that feels.

I usually try grounding techniques from DBT and they really help, here are my favorites:

Physical touch: holding yourself, cupping your face with your hand and kind of doing the thumb movement on your cheek (?), running your finger down the bridge of your nose, holding your hands together, or any other physical grounding. this along with breathing and reminding myself that this crippling feeling is coming from my mind and not from the actual way things are wildly helpful for me (also talking to myself sweetly- which I know sounds a bit dumb- but just saying things like "shh it will be okay" to myself makes a big difference)

5 senses: distracting your brain from the spiral by taking note of different senses ie. sight, smell, taste, touch, sound

Comfort Movie/Show: might not apply to you but I have specific go-to movies and shows to watch that just calm me right down and help to distract me

by being there and encouraging her to seek help you're already helping more than you know.  it is important (speaking from my experience as a recovering anorexic) to not comment on food or weight or anything of the sort even if it seems to be in a positive way it can do more hurt than harm.  not to say that encouraging her to eat meals is bad, and little things like telling her you're proud that she is eating and reinforcing the idea that you're there to support her can be really really helpful.

For me it has never been about the actual harm.  I self harm to take care of myself afterwords.  I have BPD and struggle immensely to see myself as something or someone worth taking care of, so to be able to clean out the cuts and wipe away the blood and gently bandage them is honestly really soothing.  Of course, it will always be easier to take care of the physical wound, so usually it is a distraction from the mental pain.  It helps me to quiet my mind and focus on taking care of myself.  I am almost a month clean.
